title: Equilibria
objectives: Explain reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium in terms of the rates of the forward and reverse reactions, and state that a closed system is needed
Define Le Chatelier’s principle and use it to predict the effects of changes in temperature, concentration, pressure and catalysts on an equilibrium
Deduce expressions for K<sub>c</sub> and K<sub>p</sub> (in terms of concentrations and partial pressures), including their units
Calculate K<sub>c</sub> and K<sub>p</sub>, or equilibrium quantities, from appropriate data, using mole fractions and partial pressures
Understand that K changes only with temperature, and describe the conditions used in the Haber and Contact processes
Describe Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases, conjugate acid–base pairs, and strong and weak acids and bases
Explain qualitatively the differences in behaviour of strong and weak acids, and use pH titration curves
prior: Moles, concentrations and gas calculations (Chapters 2 and 4)
Acids, alkalis and the pH scale (IGCSE)
Rates increase with temperature and concentration (IGCSE)
why: Most industrial reactions do not go to completion: they reach equilibrium. Knowing how to push an equilibrium towards the product is worth billions in ammonia and sulfuric acid production. Equilibrium calculations (K<sub>c</sub> and K<sub>p</sub>) and Le Chatelier questions appear on every Paper 1 and most Paper 2s, and the acid–base ideas continue into the A Level pH topics.
intro: In a closed system a reversible reaction reaches a state where the forward and reverse reactions go at the same rate. This chapter explains how changes in conditions shift that state, how to express it as an equilibrium constant, and how acids and bases can be described as proton donors and acceptors.

sections.title: Dynamic equilibrium and Le Chatelier’s principle

blocks.h: A reversible reaction can go in both directions (shown by ⇌). Starting from reactants, the forward rate falls as they are used up and the reverse rate rises as products build up. Eventually the two rates become equal.
The state in which the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal, so the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant. It can only be reached in a closed system.

items: The same equilibrium can be reached from either direction.

blocks.h: If a change is made to a system in dynamic equilibrium, the position of equilibrium moves to minimise (oppose) that change.

head: change
effect on position of equilibrium
effect on K
rows: shifts right (uses some of it up)
shifts to the side with fewer gas molecules; no shift if equal
K increases if forward is endothermic; decreases if exothermic
no shift; equilibrium is reached faster
add an inert gas at constant volume

blocks.name: lechat
blocks.title: Le Chatelier explorer
blocks.h: Pick a reaction and a change. The bars show the amounts before and after the new equilibrium is set up, with the reason and the effect on K.

blocks.right: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally. The yield at equilibrium is unchanged; you just get there faster.

blocks.q: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹, explain the effect of increasing the pressure and of increasing the temperature on the yield of ammonia.
steps: pressure: 4 gas molecules on the left, 2 on the right
higher pressure → shifts to the side with fewer molecules → more NH₃
temperature: forward reaction exothermic, so higher temperature favours the endothermic (reverse) direction
blocks.a: higher pressure increases the yield; higher temperature decreases the yield (and decreases K<sub>p</sub>)
blocks.err: Saying that pressure changes K: it does not.

blocks.q: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), what is the effect of doubling the pressure?
o: no change in the position of equilibrium
blocks.why: There are 2 gas molecules on each side, so pressure does not affect the position.

blocks.h: For the general equilibrium aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD:
K<sub>c</sub> = [C]<sup>c</sup>[D]<sup>d</sup> / [A]<sup>a</sup>[B]<sup>b</sup>

items: Square brackets mean concentration in mol dm⁻³ at equilibrium.
Products on top, reactants underneath; each raised to the power of its coefficient.
Pure solids are left out of the expression (in a heterogeneous equilibrium).
Work out units by cancelling: e.g. (mol dm⁻³)²/(mol dm⁻³)³ = dm³ mol⁻¹.

blocks.h: Kc changes only with temperature. If a question says K changed, the temperature changed. A large K means the equilibrium lies well to the right.
The amount of a gas divided by the total amount of gas in the mixture.
The pressure a gas in a mixture would exert if it alone occupied the whole volume: p(A) = mole fraction of A × total pressure.
for aA(g) + bB(g) ⇌ cC(g): K<sub>p</sub> = p(C)<sup>c</sup> / p(A)<sup>a</sup> p(B)<sup>b</sup>

blocks.h: Two industrial equilibria

head: Haber process
Contact process
rows: higher yield and rate; very high pressure is too costly and dangerous
yield already about 99%, so extra pressure is not worth the cost

blocks.q: Why is the temperature used in the Haber process called a compromise?
blocks.a: A low temperature gives a higher equilibrium yield (the forward reaction is exothermic) but the rate is too slow. 400–450 °C gives an acceptable yield at an acceptable rate, with the catalyst working well.

blocks.h: A proton (H⁺) donor.
A proton (H⁺) acceptor.
When an acid donates a proton, what is left is its conjugate base. When a base accepts a proton, it becomes its conjugate acid. The two members of a pair differ by one H⁺.

summary: Dynamic equilibrium: forward and reverse rates equal; concentrations constant; closed system.
Le Chatelier: the position of equilibrium moves to oppose a change.
Pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules; temperature rise favours the endothermic direction; catalysts do not move the position.
Only temperature changes K. Exothermic forward reaction: K decreases as T increases.
Use an equilibrium table: initial, change (from the equation ratio), equilibrium; divide by volume for K<sub>c</sub>.
Mole fraction = moles of gas ÷ total moles; partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure.
K<sub>p</sub> uses partial pressures; units come from the difference in gas moles.
Haber: 400–450 °C, 200 atm, Fe catalyst. Contact: 400–450 °C, 1–2 atm, V₂O₅ catalyst.
Brønsted–Lowry acid = proton donor; base = proton acceptor; conjugate pairs differ by one H⁺.
Strong acids/bases fully dissociate; weak ones only partially. Strength is not concentration.
Titration curves: strong–strong steep from about 3 to 11; weak acid–strong base equivalence above 7; strong acid–weak base below 7.

practice.q: Write K<sub>c</sub>, with units, for 2NO(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g).

Explain why the Contact process uses only 1–2 atm even though higher pressure would increase the yield.
practice.a: The equilibrium yield is already very high (about 99%) at low pressure, so higher pressure would add cost and danger for little gain.

practice.a: total 1.00 mol; p(PCl₅) 10, p(PCl₃) 20, p(Cl₂) 20 atm; K<sub>p</sub> = 20 × 20/10 = 40 atm

assessment_s.q:
Hydrogen and iodine react: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g).
(a) Write the expression for Kc. [1]
(b) 0.50 mol H₂ and 0.50 mol I₂ are heated in a 2.0 dm³ vessel. At equilibrium 0.80 mol HI is present. Calculate Kc. [3]
(c) Explain why Kc for this reaction has no units and why its value does not depend on the volume. [2]
assessment_s.a:
(a) Kc = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂])
(b) H₂ = I₂ = 0.10 mol; concentrations 0.050, 0.050, 0.40; Kc = 0.40²/(0.050 × 0.050) = 64
(c) the concentration units cancel ((mol dm⁻³)²/(mol dm⁻³)²); equal numbers of moles on each side, so the volume cancels

assessment_s.q:
Propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH, is a weak Brønsted–Lowry acid.
(a) Write an equation for its reaction with water and identify the conjugate base. [2]
(b) Explain the difference between a strong acid and a weak acid. [1]
(c) Sketch and describe the pH curve when 0.10 mol dm⁻³ NaOH is added to 25 cm³ of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ propanoic acid. [2]
assessment_s.a:
(a) CH₃CH₂COOH + H₂O ⇌ CH₃CH₂COO⁻ + H₃O⁺; conjugate base CH₃CH₂COO⁻
(b) a strong acid dissociates fully in water; a weak acid only partially
(c) starts near pH 3, rises gently, steep section from about 7 to 11 at 25 cm³, equivalence pH above 7, levels at about 13

pp.skill: Features of dynamic equilibrium
pp.mis: Thinking the reactions stop or the concentrations become equal
pp.stem: Which statement about a reaction mixture at dynamic equilibrium is correct?
opts: The concentrations of reactants and products are equal.
The forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates.
It can only be reached in an open container.
pp.exp: At dynamic equilibrium both reactions keep going at the same rate, so the concentrations stay constant (but are not usually equal). It needs a closed system.

pp.skill: Le Chatelier: conditions that increase yield
pp.mis: Thinking a catalyst increases yield
pp.stem:
N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) ΔH = +58 kJ mol⁻¹
What increases the equilibrium yield of NO₂?
pp.exp: The forward reaction is endothermic, so a higher temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right. Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules (N₂O₄). A catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium.

pp.skill: Choosing conditions when gas moles are equal on both sides
pp.mis: Assuming pressure always matters
pp.stem:
CO(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO₂(g) + H₂(g) ΔH = −41 kJ mol⁻¹
Which conditions give the highest equilibrium yield of hydrogen?
opts: high pressure only, at any temperature
pp.exp: There are 2 mol of gas on each side, so pressure has no effect on the position of equilibrium. The forward reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature favours the products.

pp.skill: Statements about an exothermic gas equilibrium
pp.mis: Writing Kp without the powers from the equation
pp.stem:
2NO(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) ΔH = −114 kJ mol⁻¹
Which statement is correct?
opts: Increasing the pressure increases the equilibrium yield of NO₂.
Increasing the temperature increases the equilibrium yield of NO₂.
A catalyst increases the equilibrium yield of NO₂.
pp.exp: 3 mol of gas on the left, 2 on the right: higher pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right. K<sub>p</sub> = p(NO₂)² / [p(NO)² × p(O₂)]. The reaction is exothermic, so higher temperature lowers the yield. Catalysts do not change yield.

pp.skill: Separating rate effects from equilibrium effects
pp.mis: Confusing faster with more product
pp.stem: The reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) is exothermic. Which statement is correct?
opts: A catalyst increases the percentage of SO₃ at equilibrium.
A higher temperature increases the percentage of SO₃ at equilibrium.
A higher temperature increases the rates of both the forward and the reverse reactions.
Increasing the pressure decreases the rate of the forward reaction.
pp.exp: Raising the temperature speeds up both reactions (more molecules have energy ≥ E<sub>a</sub>), even though it moves the equilibrium to the left. Higher pressure increases the rate (more frequent collisions).

pp.skill: Interpreting yield data at different temperatures and pressures
pp.mis: Thinking higher pressure changes K
pp.stem: For the reaction A(g) + 2B(g) ⇌ C(g), the equilibrium percentage of C is shown at different conditions. Which statement is correct?
pp.exp: Yield falls as the temperature rises, so the forward reaction is exothermic and K<sub>p</sub> falls with temperature. Yield rises with pressure because there are fewer gas molecules on the right, but K<sub>p</sub> depends only on temperature.

pp.skill: Predicting the shape of yield–pressure graphs
pp.mis: Placing the higher-temperature line above
pp.stem: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) is exothermic. Graphs are drawn of % SO₃ at equilibrium against pressure, at 400 °C and at 600 °C. Which description is correct?
opts: Both lines rise with pressure; the 400 °C line is above the 600 °C line.
Both lines rise with pressure; the 600 °C line is above the 400 °C line.
Both lines fall with pressure; the 400 °C line is above the 600 °C line.
Both lines are flat; pressure has no effect.
pp.exp: Fewer gas molecules on the right: % SO₃ rises with pressure. Exothermic: the lower temperature gives the higher yield at every pressure.

pp.skill: Deducing a change of conditions from a change in K
pp.mis: Thinking pressure changes K
pp.stem: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) ΔH = −197 kJ mol⁻¹. Under one set of conditions K<sub>p</sub> = 3.0 × 10⁴ atm⁻¹. After a change of conditions, K<sub>p</sub> = 1.2 atm⁻¹. What change was made?
pp.exp: Only temperature changes the value of an equilibrium constant. K<sub>p</sub> became smaller, so the equilibrium moved to the left: for an exothermic reaction, that happens when the temperature is raised.

pp.skill: Predicting rates when two conditions change together
pp.mis: Predicting the equilibrium shift when the effects compete
pp.stem: A mixture of SO₂, O₂ and SO₃ at equilibrium at 700 K (exothermic forward reaction) is transferred into a much smaller sealed vessel kept at 900 K. Which prediction can be made with certainty?
opts: The position of equilibrium will not change.
A dynamic equilibrium will not be re-established.
The rate of the reverse reaction will decrease.
The rate of the forward reaction will increase.
pp.exp: Higher concentrations and a higher temperature both make the forward reaction faster. The effects on the position of equilibrium compete (higher pressure → right; higher temperature → left), so we cannot be sure which way it moves.

pp.skill: Effect of an inert gas at constant volume
pp.mis: Thinking extra total pressure shifts the equilibrium
pp.stem: An equilibrium mixture N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) is in a sealed vessel of fixed volume at constant temperature. Neon is pumped in. Predict what happens to the forward rate and to the equilibrium partial pressure of NO₂.
pp.exp: At constant volume the amounts and concentrations of N₂O₄ and NO₂ do not change, so neither their partial pressures nor the rates change. Only the total pressure rises.

pp.skill: Common-ion effect on a solid in equilibrium
pp.mis: Forgetting that H⁺ removes F⁻
pp.stem:
CaF₂(s) ⇌ Ca²⁺(aq) + 2F⁻(aq)
Which substance, when added, increases the amount of solid CaF₂?
pp.exp: Extra F⁻ shifts the equilibrium to the left, so more CaF₂ precipitates. HCl removes F⁻ (forming HF), shifting it right. NaCl has no common ion; more water dissolves more solid.

pp.skill: New equilibrium concentration after adding a reactant
pp.mis: Thinking the equilibrium removes all the added reactant
pp.stem: X(aq) + Y(aq) ⇌ Z(aq). In 1.0 dm³ of an equilibrium mixture, [X] = 4.0 mol dm⁻³. Then 2.0 mol of X is dissolved in the mixture without changing its volume. What is [X] when equilibrium is restored?
pp.exp: The equilibrium shifts right and uses up some, but not all, of the added X (Le Chatelier only partly opposes the change). So [X] ends between 4.0 and 6.0 mol dm⁻³.

pp.skill: Units of K<sub>c</sub>
pp.mis: Counting the number of species rather than concentration terms
pp.stem: All species are in aqueous solution. For which reaction does K<sub>c</sub> have the units dm³ mol⁻¹?
pp.exp: K<sub>c</sub> = [Y]/([W][X]): (mol dm⁻³)/(mol dm⁻³)² = dm³ mol⁻¹. B and D give mol dm⁻³; C has no units.

pp.skill: Writing K<sub>c</sub> with equilibrium amounts
pp.mis: Using initial amounts
pp.stem: 0.30 mol of H₂ and 0.25 mol of I₂ are heated in a sealed vessel. At equilibrium there is 0.40 mol of HI. H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). Which expression gives K<sub>c</sub>?
pp.exp: Forming 0.40 mol HI uses 0.20 mol H₂ and 0.20 mol I₂, leaving 0.10 and 0.05 mol. The volume cancels because both sides have 2 mol in total. K<sub>c</sub> = 0.40² / (0.10 × 0.05) = 32.

pp.skill: K<sub>c</sub> for an esterification
pp.mis: Not squaring by using only one product
pp.stem: A carboxylic acid and an alcohol form an ester and water. 0.50 mol of the acid and 0.50 mol of the alcohol are mixed. At equilibrium 0.30 mol of ester is present. What is K<sub>c</sub>?
pp.exp: At equilibrium: acid 0.20, alcohol 0.20, ester 0.30, water 0.30 mol. K<sub>c</sub> = (0.30 × 0.30) / (0.20 × 0.20) = 2.25 (no units; the volumes cancel).

pp.skill: K<sub>c</sub> when a product is present at the start
pp.mis: Ignoring the water added initially
pp.stem:
ROH(l) + CH₃COOH(l) ⇌ CH₃COOR(l) + H₂O(l)
2.0 mol ROH, 2.0 mol CH₃COOH and 0.5 mol H₂O are mixed. At equilibrium, 1.2 mol of ester is present. What is Kc?

wrong.C: forgot the 0.5 mol of water present initially

pp.skill: K<sub>c</sub> from a mass of product
pp.mis: Using moles instead of concentrations
pp.stem: 1.00 mol of SO₃ is heated in a 5.00 dm³ vessel: 2SO₃(g) ⇌ 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g). At equilibrium the mixture contains 6.40 g of O₂. What is K<sub>c</sub>?

pp.skill: K<sub>c</sub> for a heterogeneous equilibrium
pp.mis: Including the solid in the expression
pp.stem: Solid ammonium hydrogensulfide is heated in a 2.00 dm³ container: NH₄HS(s) ⇌ NH₃(g) + H₂S(g). Initially there is 1.00 mol of NH₄HS; at equilibrium 0.400 mol remains. What is the numerical value of K<sub>c</sub>?
pp.exp: 0.600 mol of each gas forms, so [NH₃] = [H₂S] = 0.300 mol dm⁻³. Solids are left out of K<sub>c</sub>: K<sub>c</sub> = 0.300 × 0.300 = 0.0900.

wrong.C: divided by the "concentration" of the solid

pp.skill: Setting up K<sub>c</sub> from an equilibrium table
pp.mis: Forgetting to divide by the volume
pp.stem: 3.0 mol of HI is placed in a 2.0 dm³ vessel and heated: 2HI(g) ⇌ H₂(g) + I₂(g). At equilibrium there is 0.40 mol of H₂. Which expression gives K<sub>c</sub>?
pp.exp: H₂ = I₂ = 0.40 mol; HI = 3.0 − 0.80 = 2.2 mol. Concentrations: 0.20, 0.20 and 1.1 mol dm⁻³. K<sub>c</sub> = (0.20 × 0.20)/1.1² = 0.033.

pp.skill: Equilibrium amounts from the stoichiometry
pp.mis: Ignoring the 1 : 2 ratio
pp.stem: 2.0 mol of N₂O₄ is placed in a container. N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂. At equilibrium 1.4 mol of N₂O₄ remains. What amount of NO₂ is present?
pp.exp: 0.6 mol of N₂O₄ reacted, giving 2 × 0.6 = 1.2 mol NO₂.

pp.skill: Equilibrium amount from a given K<sub>c</sub>
pp.mis: Forgetting the factor of 2 for HI
pp.stem: 1.0 mol of H₂ and 1.0 mol of I₂ are placed in a 1.0 dm³ sealed container. H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g); K<sub>c</sub> = 16. What amount of HI is present at equilibrium?
pp.exp: Let x mol of H₂ react: (2x)²/(1 − x)² = 16, so 2x/(1 − x) = 4, giving x = 2/3. HI = 2x = 1.33 mol.

pp.skill: New equilibrium concentrations after a temperature change
pp.mis: Changing H₂ by the full drop in HI
pp.stem: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) ΔH = −9.6 kJ mol⁻¹. At equilibrium [H₂] = 0.50, [I₂] = 0.50 and [HI] = 3.00 mol dm⁻³. The temperature is raised at constant volume and the new equilibrium [HI] is 2.60 mol dm⁻³. What is the new [H₂]?
pp.exp: HI fell by 0.40, so 0.20 mol dm⁻³ each of H₂ and I₂ formed: [H₂] = 0.50 + 0.20 = 0.70 mol dm⁻³. (The exothermic reaction shifts left as the temperature rises.)

pp.skill: Finding K<sub>c</sub> when two concentrations are equal
pp.mis: Not raising the concentration to its power
pp.stem: A(aq) + 2B(aq) ⇌ AB₂(aq). When [B] = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ at equilibrium, [A] = [AB₂]. What is the numerical value of K<sub>c</sub>?

pp.skill: Equilibrium concentration from the percentage reacted
pp.mis: Using moles instead of concentration
pp.stem: 4.10 g of sodium ethanoate, CH₃COONa (M<sub>r</sub> 82.0), is dissolved to make 500 cm³ of solution. CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COOH(aq) + OH⁻(aq). At equilibrium, 0.010% of the ethanoate ions have reacted. What is [CH₃COOH]?

wrong.A: this is the amount in moles
wrong.C: used 0.010 as the fraction instead of 0.00010

pp.skill: Units of K<sub>p</sub>
pp.mis: Not counting gas moles on each side
pp.stem: For which equilibrium does K<sub>p</sub> have the units atm⁻¹?
pp.exp: Units = atm^(moles of gas on the right − moles on the left). B: 2 − 3 = −1, so atm⁻¹. A: 0 (no units); C: +1 (atm); D: −2 (atm⁻²).

pp.skill: K<sub>p</sub> expression and industrial conditions for the Haber process
pp.mis: Mixing up the Haber and Contact conditions
pp.stem: Which row gives the K<sub>p</sub> expression and the temperature used for the Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)?
pp.exp: Each partial pressure is raised to its coefficient, products over reactants. The Haber process runs at about 400–450 °C and 200 atm (about 20 000 kPa) with an iron catalyst: a compromise between rate and yield.

pp.skill: K<sub>p</sub> from equilibrium amounts and total pressure
pp.mis: Using amounts instead of partial pressures
pp.stem: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g). An equilibrium mixture at a total pressure of 10.0 atm contains 2.0 mol SO₂, 3.0 mol O₂ and 15.0 mol SO₃. What is K<sub>p</sub>?
pp.exp: Total = 20.0 mol. Partial pressures: SO₂ 1.0, O₂ 1.5, SO₃ 7.5 atm. K<sub>p</sub> = 7.5² / (1.0² × 1.5) = 37.5 atm⁻¹.

wrong.C: used moles instead of partial pressures

pp.skill: K<sub>p</sub> in terms of the total pressure
pp.mis: Forgetting to square the product term
pp.stem: X(g) ⇌ 2Y(g). At equilibrium the total pressure is p and the partial pressure of X is p/3. What is K<sub>p</sub>?

pp.skill: Partial pressure from the fraction reacted
pp.mis: Forgetting that the total amount of gas changes
pp.stem: N₂ and H₂ are mixed in the ratio 1 : 3. At equilibrium, 25% of the N₂ has reacted and the total pressure is p. What is the partial pressure of NH₃?
pp.exp: Start 1 : 3. React 0.25 N₂ and 0.75 H₂, forming 0.50 NH₃. Equilibrium: 0.75 + 2.25 + 0.50 = 3.50 mol. Mole fraction of NH₃ = 0.50/3.50 = 1/7.

pp.skill: Mole fractions and partial pressures from an equilibrium amount
pp.mis: Assuming the total amount of gas changes when it does not
pp.stem: 1.0 mol of H₂ and 1.5 mol of I₂ are heated in a closed container: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). At equilibrium there is 1.6 mol of HI. Which statement is correct?
opts: The partial pressure of H₂ is greater than that of I₂.
The mole fraction of HI is 0.64.
The total amount of gas at equilibrium is greater than at the start.
pp.exp: H₂ = 0.2, I₂ = 0.7, HI = 1.6: total 2.5 mol (unchanged). Mole fraction of HI = 1.6/2.5 = 0.64. p(I₂) > p(H₂). K<sub>p</sub> has no units.

pp.skill: Facts about the Haber and Contact processes
pp.mis: Thinking a catalyst or pressure changes K<sub>p</sub>
pp.stem: Which statement about the Haber and Contact processes is correct?
opts: The iron catalyst in the Haber process does not change the value of K<sub>p</sub>.
K<sub>p</sub> for the Contact process has the units atm.
Increasing the pressure in the Haber process increases K<sub>p</sub>.
The Contact process uses a homogeneous catalyst.
pp.exp: Catalysts speed up both reactions equally, so K<sub>p</sub> and the position of equilibrium are unchanged. K<sub>p</sub> (Contact) has units atm⁻¹. Only temperature changes K<sub>p</sub>. V₂O₅ is a solid catalyst for gases: heterogeneous.

pp.skill: Adding a common ion to a weak base equilibrium
pp.mis: Forgetting that [OH⁻] falling makes pH fall
pp.stem: Aqueous ammonia: NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq). Solid ammonium chloride is dissolved in it. What happens to [OH⁻] and the pH?
pp.exp: Extra NH₄⁺ shifts the equilibrium to the left, so [OH⁻] falls. The solution becomes less alkaline: the pH decreases.

pp.skill: Factors that change the pH of a weak acid solution
pp.mis: Thinking a catalyst changes pH
pp.stem:
NH₄⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₃(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq) ΔH = +52 kJ mol⁻¹
Which change causes the pH of aqueous ammonium chloride to decrease?
opts: dissolving a little ammonia in the solution
pp.exp: The forward reaction is endothermic, so heating shifts it right: [H₃O⁺] rises and the pH falls. NaOH removes H₃O⁺; added NH₃ shifts it left; a catalyst has no effect on position.

pp.skill: Shape of a strong alkali–weak acid titration curve
pp.mis: Expecting the steep section to be centred on pH 7
pp.stem: A weak acid is added from a burette to a strong alkali until the acid is in excess. Which description of the pH curve is correct?
opts: starts near pH 1, rises steeply around pH 7, ends near pH 13
starts near pH 13, falls steeply from about pH 11 to 7, ends around pH 3
starts near pH 13, falls steeply from about pH 11 to 3, ends near pH 1
starts near pH 11, falls gradually with no steep section
pp.exp: The alkali is in the flask, so the pH starts high (about 13). Near the end-point it drops sharply, but only to about pH 7 because the weak acid gives an alkaline salt. In excess weak acid the pH stays around 3, not 1.

pp.skill: Identifying an acid and alkali from a titration curve
pp.mis: Ignoring the volume at the end-point
pp.stem: 20 cm³ of acid P is titrated with alkali Q of the same concentration (mol dm⁻³). The curve starts at pH 1, the steep section goes from about pH 3 to pH 11, and the end-point is at 40 cm³ of Q. Which row identifies P and Q?
pp.exp: Twice the volume of alkali is needed, so each acid molecule gives 2 H⁺: H₂SO₄ with NaOH. Strong acid + strong base: steep section from about 3 to 11. With Ba(OH)₂ only 10 cm³ would be needed.
